How the day works

Your car was loaded this morning in delivery order. Each label carries a stop number and a shelf code: R is the curb side, L the street side, sections 1–8 run from the cab to the rear door, then TOP / MID / BOT. Letters ride in the bin up front. Heavy pieces sit on the floor by the rear door. The preload isn't perfect, so now and then a piece is in the wrong bay.

W A S DDrive (arrows work too). Hold S to brake, then reverse. SpaceSet or release the parking brake. Stop first. EOpen the cargo hold (parked only). Click pieces to pick them up. Click a houseWalk to that door with what you're carrying. Click several to deliver a loop. FWalk to the targeted stop, or call yourself back to the truck. N / BNext or previous stop on the handheld. L opens the full stop list. CSwitch between chase, high and overhead cameras. Mouse wheel or +/- zooms. MRoute map. H horn. Esc menu.

Red-striped labels have a deadline (most are 10:30). Blue S means a signature is required. Businesses keep hours; the diner and bakery close early, the theater opens late. Afternoon pickups show up on the board, and Dale on the radio may add more or bump a stop up. Avenues stop at every crossing, and so does Main St downtown. Country roads are faster but watch for cows. Dogs, odd neighbors and unhappy customers turn up at the door: pick how you handle them.

Every day brings its own weather. Rain and snow mean longer stops and slides, and fog shrinks what you can see. Orange barricades close a few streets, so plan detours (they show on the map). Some customers leave delivery notes on the handheld; read them before you walk up. After three, a school bus runs near the school, and red lights mean you stop. A freight line runs along Quarry Rd: when the gates come down, wait. Downtown crosswalks fill up with school classes, walking clubs and the occasional family of ducks, and cyclists share the road, so give them room. Parked cars narrow the side streets, so ease toward the center line to get around them, like you would in a real truck. Mailboxes, trash cans, signs, fences and yard things break if you hit them, and Dale hears about every one. Houses and stores don't break, but hitting one hard leaves a hole in the wall, a long talk with your supervisor and twenty minutes off your day. The crews put everything back overnight. Clock out at the Delivery Center to get paid and add the day to your career.

PACKAGE
CAR

Cedar Bend has a village, a strip of shops and warehouses, a freight line, and a long stretch of farms, forest and lake roads, all in 3D and full of neighbors going about their day. Every morning the car leaves the center with a fresh, random load of about a hundred and forty stops. Drive the route, set the brake, find the piece, walk it to the door. Mind the dogs, humor the locals, keep the customers happy, and answer Dale on the radio.
